title: Promises in the Ruins
body: An argument in a courtroom

Nuremberg, November 1945. Twenty-one senior Nazi officials sat in the dock; one more was tried in absentia. They faced an unprecedented tribunal. Hermann Göring wore a gray suit. He had lost considerable weight, but seemed much clearer-headed than during the war, answering questions with coherent, even sharp logic.

When the prosecution accused him of crimes against humanity, the line of defense was simple: I was a government official carrying out state policy and obeying state law. By what right could representatives of other states judge me?

Before Nuremberg, international law revolved mainly around states, and international criminal accountability for national leaders was particularly weak. But individual responsibility did not begin at Nuremberg. Individual liability for war crimes had precedents, and attempts at accountability after the First World War had already raised the issue, though their enforcement was extremely limited.

Nuremberg advanced this principle to a new level: senior state officials, too, had to face individual responsibility. A person could not merely say that they were carrying out state policy and transfer all responsibility to the state. Institutional identity could not serve as a passport to immunity.

This was a turning point in institutional history. An international tribunal subjected senior national officials to individual criminal accountability. Between system and person, it articulated a principle: people cannot hide behind the system.
A breakthrough
Seen against the long sweep of history, the principles established at Nuremberg were momentous.

First, individuals must answer for their actions even when carrying out superior orders or state policy. Institutional identity is no pass into a moral vacuum. Putting on a uniform does not release someone from being human.

Second, there is law beyond national law: crimes against humanity. A state may enact laws through its own legal system, but when those laws produce systematic extermination and persecution, they cannot shield those who carry them out from accountability.

Third, state sovereignty is not absolute. What a state does to its own citizens is no longer purely an “internal affair.” The international community has a right, at least in principle, to intervene and to judge.

Together, these principles point in one direction: institutions are not the final end. Human dignity and life stand above them. When institutions systematically destroy that dignity and life, their authority ceases to hold.
But the breakthrough was real, and so were its limits. Those limits were not technical imperfections. They were structural contradictions.

The most obvious: Nuremberg was a victors' tribunal. Those in the dock were all officials of the defeated state. Nobody was tried there for Dresden. Nobody was tried for Hiroshima. Nobody was tried for the Bengal famine. Soviet judges sat on the bench while millions remained in the Soviet Gulag.

The essay must therefore ask: why were the actions of the side that bombed Dresden not examined under the same principles? This question deserves serious consideration. But questioning the selectivity of the trials does not lessen the guilt of Göring and other responsible Nazi figures.

Nuremberg drew its legitimacy from military victory, not from a moral authority standing above all belligerents. The lofty principles it proclaimed, individual responsibility, crimes against humanity, limits to sovereignty, were therefore selectively applied from the beginning. The principles were universal; their application was asymmetrical.

The contradiction was structural. A justice system established by the victors could not put the victors themselves on trial. An unbridgeable gap separated the source of its power, military victory, from the source of its legitimacy, moral principles transcending all states.
Nuremberg tried to write “the person stands above the system” into institutional life. But the pen was held by the systems that had won the war.
A declaration's light and its limits

On December 10, 1948, the United Nations General Assembly adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. Eleanor Roosevelt chaired both the Commission on Human Rights and the formal drafting committee. The Commission had eighteen members; the formal drafting committee comprised representatives of eight countries: China, France, Lebanon, the Soviet Union, Britain, Australia, Chile, and the United States. During more than two years of drafting, participants argued repeatedly over every word.
Article 1 of the final text reads: “All human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights.”

It is hard to overstate the weight of that sentence in human civilization. No earlier global document had declared that every person, regardless of nationality, race, sex, or belief, possessed inalienable dignity simply by being human. This was not the declaration of a single cultural tradition, the teaching of a single religion, or the constitution of a single state. It was humanity, taken as a whole, attempting for the first time to affirm at an institutional level that people are ends.
Then came the question: who would ensure that these words were honored?

The Universal Declaration was adopted by the General Assembly. It was not a treaty for states to sign and ratify. The 1948 declaration itself established no independent mechanism of coercive enforcement. It set out a common standard without simultaneously creating a power sufficient to guarantee compliance.

Later, its principles gradually entered international treaties, domestic law, and customary international law, acquiring real legal effect. Yet a long road still separates writing a principle into law from making it part of someone's life.

Here is the difficulty: human rights need institutions to protect them, but the states able to establish those institutions may themselves be violating rights. Constraints are not impossible to build. But every step toward them encounters resistance from power and selective enforcement.
The declaration is a remarkable signpost. Later laws and institutions have built some roads in the direction it points. Those roads remain far from reaching everyone.
The United Nations: an honest compromise

The designers of the United Nations were more candid than those of the League. The League pretended that great powers would submit to the collective will, then looked away when they did not. The UN wrote their special status directly into its Charter: the five permanent members of the Security Council have a veto.

This was a pragmatic choice. The logic was straightforward: better a United Nations that kept the great powers inside by granting privileges than one that held to principle while the great powers walked out. The latter had been the League's fate. The designers did not want to repeat it.
Judged by institutional survival, the design has been highly successful. The United Nations has existed for more than eighty years, over three times the League's twenty-six.

But what is the price of that survival? From the beginning, the institution accepted that not everyone's security would carry equal weight. Citizens of permanent-member states stand behind governments with veto power; others do not. When the Security Council considers responding to genocide, a permanent member that regards intervention as contrary to its interests can obstruct action, whether through a formal veto or less visible means.
During the 1994 Rwandan genocide, the Security Council failed to take effective action, leaving hundreds of thousands to be murdered within a hundred days.

The UN has outlasted the League because it learned a lesson: do not act beyond what the great powers will tolerate. Their tolerance is defined more often by their own systemic interests than by the principle that people are ends.

This is not merely a “flaw” in the UN. It is a condition of its existence. Remove that condition, and the UN would probably repeat the League's fate. Retain it, and the UN can never fully honor its promise of equality. Another crack. Better than none, but still not large or wide enough.
Selective repair
The most revealing question about postwar reconstruction is not what was done, but for whom.

The Marshall Plan injected more than thirteen billion dollars into Western Europe, roughly a hundred and fifty billion in today's terms, rebuilding economic infrastructure and laying foundations for European integration. West Germany rose from the ruins to become the world's third-largest economy within twenty years.

Yet Britain, France, the Netherlands, Belgium, and Portugal were maintaining colonial rule in the same period. Some governments that supported the Universal Declaration at the UN were also suppressing independence movements in their colonies. France fought an eight-year bloody colonial war in Algeria. Britain used detention camps during the Mau Mau uprising in Kenya.

On one side, “All human beings are born free.” On the other, colonized peoples did not even have the right to govern themselves. The contradiction was more than hypocrisy. It had a deeper structural cause: the builders of the postwar order were themselves systems, unable to establish an institution that would truly scrutinize their own conduct.

The Marshall Plan was never solely about “giving Europeans a better life.” It was also a move in the Cold War, a strategic investment to keep Western Europe from turning toward the Soviet Union. Preserving colonies likewise served systemic interests: raw materials, markets, strategic positions.

Postwar repair was therefore stratified. People at the system's center, in Western Europe, received comprehensive reconstruction and recognition of rights. Those on its margins, in the colonies, were made to wait, subjected to conditions, or ignored altogether.

Decolonization partly corrected this asymmetry. By the 1960s, most colonies had gained political independence. But political independence is not economic independence; a changed flag does not guarantee a changed structure. Many people in postcolonial states went from being instruments of an imperial power to instruments in another part of the global economy. Instrumentalization changed its face and continued.
A paradox the size of a nuclear bomb
If one thing could encapsulate the contradictions of the postwar order, it would be nuclear weapons.

Nuclear deterrence works by staking the capacity to destroy humanity against maintaining a condition of non-war between two superpowers. Throughout the Cold War, humanity lived under the shadow of possible extinction at any moment. During the Cuban missile crisis, “any moment” nearly became “this moment.”

It also “worked.” There was no Third World War, and very few people died in direct conflict between the superpowers, though more than ten million died in proxy wars. “It works” is deterrence's strongest defense.

From the standpoint of people as ends, that very “usefulness” becomes the deepest indictment. What does it mean when a system must stake humanity's survival in order to operate? It means that the system takes its own equilibrium as its end, not human beings. People are not those being protected, but hostages. The hostage-taker is not one identifiable villain, but the logic of the system itself.
And this is called “peace.”
Light and shadow
Institution-building after 1945 cannot be assessed with a simple verdict.

On one side, humanity had never come so far. Nuremberg advanced individual criminal accountability for senior state officials to a new level, preventing institutional identity from being sufficient to conceal personal responsibility. Before the Universal Declaration, no global document had recognized each person's dignity simply as a human being. Before the UN, no enduring global institution had at least in theory promised all states an equal place. These were real achievements.

On the other side, each achievement carried structural limits. Nuremberg's justice was selective. The promises expressed in the declaration still lacked sufficient and equal guarantees of realization. UN equality made an exception for veto power. And nuclear deterrence, the order's ultimate guarantee, was itself an extreme form of holding people hostage.

Perhaps the most accurate summary is this: after 1945, humanity wrote “people are ends” into its institutions for the first time. But the institutional order containing those words did not itself operate with people as its end. The promise was real, and its realization remained far from universal. Both things were true at once, without contradiction.

Because “people are ends” is not a condition that institutions can declare and thereby automatically achieve. It needs cracks: cracks permitting dissent, cracks permitting correction. Nuremberg, the declaration, the UN did not finish a building. They opened a few cracks in an enormous wall.
Light comes through the cracks. The wall remains.
deck: Nuremberg, human rights, the United Nations: real advances whose institutional limits remain.
